raw: Hello Daniil, come in, have a seat. Where would you like to start today?
I don't really know. My general practitioner suggested I come. She said I look exhausted and she's right. I am.
What does exhausted look like for you?
Like I'm running on fumes. I work as a project manager at a logistics company and I've been completely burnt out since October.
Since October, did something happen then?
Not one thing. We lost a big client, half of the team got moved onto the rescue plan, so I ended up doing three people's jobs. Just never came back after that.
What does a normal working day look for you now?
I'm at my desk by 7 and I'm still answering messages at 10 at night. Even when I'm not working, I'm thinking about work.
That's a very long day. How was your sleep?
Terrible. Most nights I sleep about 4 hours. I wake up at 3 in the morning and just can't fall back asleep.
What happens when you wake at 3am?
My head just starts. Shipping schedules, the client, whether I've forgotten something. Then I look at the clock and I do the math on how little sleep I'm gonna get, which makes it worse.
And then...
Then I lie until about 5 and get up and make tea. I've started dreading the nights, if I'm honest.
That sounds draining. Is there anything else going on in your life besides work?
Yeah, my father. He was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in the autumn.
That's a lot to carry alongside everything else. How is he?
He's still himself, mostly. His hands shake, he's slower, he gets frustrated. He's having a dream and he's always being just someone.
And how are you involved in his care?
I'm the one who drives them to the hospital in Leeds. Neurology appointments are every few weeks. It's about an hour each way.
Is there anybody who shares that with you?
Not really. My younger sister Hannah lives in Toronto so we'll have to care for our father who falls on me.
How do you feel about that?
Guilty for even saying it. She calls him every Sunday. She's not the one who's neglecting him. Just I'm the one who's here.
Can you say more about the girl?
He feels selfish to be tired when he's the one he's ill, so I don't say anything to anyone.
Not to a honoured eater.
She asks how I am, l'est-ce-fine? What would be the point? She can't do anything from Canada.
What would you want her to know if you said it?
I'm not fine that some days I sit in a car park at the hospital for 10 minutes before I go in because I can't face it.
That's an important thing to notice, what happens in those 10 minutes.
Nothing really, just breathe and look at every people going in. Everybody looks tired here.
You mentioned your GP. What did she say?
She had blood tests. They were all normal. She said it's stress and exhaustion. If I asked about talking to someone, they said I hadn't got the time.
And yet, you are here.
A girlfriend booked her to be honest. She said she was done watching me disappear.
How is it with Claire?
She's very patient. She makes me tea and doesn't push me to talk. But I can see she's wearing a hood too.
In a wonderful way.
She stopped asking if I wanted to go away for the weekend because I always said no. That's the thing I feel worst about actually.
What stops you from saying yes?
The emails and the family will come back to 200 of them and that might need something.
So even rest has a price.
Yeah, exactly. Can't remember the last time I was properly off.
What did you do for yourself before October?
We run on Globetrus every Saturday morning. We've done it for six years.
And now...
I stopped about two months ago. My legs feel like lead and I just never went back.
How do you feel about that?
I feel like I've lost a part of myself. It was the one time in the week nobody could reach me.
What would it mean to get some of that back?
A lot probably. I just can't picture the time that would come from.
Let's leave that for a moment. What is your relationship with your boss?
Peterson, he's alright as a person, but he sends emails at 11 at night and expects an answer before breakfast.
What do you do when one arrives?
I answer it every time, even if I'm in bed. Claire hates it.
What are you afraid would happen if you didn't answer?
The client says that he doesn't want to be in a relationship with a therapist.
End of day.
The client talks about family, work, sleep, anxiety and feelings.
Both things can be true.
The therapist says, I'm not sure. I suppose so. I've never said that out.
Who are your moves apart from the tiredness?
But mostly. And irritable. He slept at a colleague last week or nothing and went and sat in the toilets for 10 minutes.
What was happening for you in those minutes?
Her heart was going and my hands were shaking. We thought for a second it was a heart attack but it passed.
Has it happened before?
A couple of times. Once on a train to Manchester, just to get off and stand on a platform.
That sounds frightening.
It was. I hadn't told anyone about it, not even Claire.
Thank you for telling me. What are you afraid means?
I'm losing it. I'm going to end up like, I don't know, coping.
Have you noticed anything that makes it worse?
Coffee, probably. I want about six cups a day and I've started having wine in the evenings to switch my head off. Two glasses, sometimes three.
How do you feel about falling?
The therapist says,
You are noticing that clearly that is useful.
It doesn't feel useful. Feels like I'm listing everything that's wrong with me.
I hear a person who has been holding a great deal on his own for a long time. What was it like to say it today?
Strange. A bit of relief actually. Like putting on a bag and a trill ice I was carrying.
What do you carry when you would like to put down first?
The nights, I think. If I could sleep, I could probably call blood to rest.
We can start there. The thing about your family growing up, shape, how you handled it.
My grandfather worked at the mines in Yorkshire. He never complained about anything. Not once. That's the same. Just get on with it.
And you?
The client says he's been here for a week.
What would you say to him if he were here?

The client says, I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired. I'm tired.
That sounds like something you could say to yourself as well.
Maybe. I don't know if I believe it yet.
That's fine, you don't have to. Let's think about what we could do between now and next week. Would you be willing to try something small?
The client talks about family, work, sleep, anxiety and feelings.
Very small. A fixed time in the evening when you switch off your phone, even for 20 minutes.
The person would hate that.
What would actually happen in 20 minutes?
I think, probably, he wouldn't even notice.
Would you try it?
Yeah, half past nine, perhaps. I could make it at Dango's Glare.
That sounds good. And a note of how the night goes.
I can do that right down when I wake up, if I wake up.
We're nearly out of time. How are you feeling right now?
The client says that the client is feeling a little bit shaky.
It takes energy to say it loud loud.
Alright, thank you. I think I needed to hear that.
Same time next week.
Yeah, I'll be here. I'll try to make it on time. The trains are awful.
